screens.title: Using Quartus Prime for FPGA Development
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll develop a practical workflow for using Intel Quartus Prime to build and deploy FPGA designs. We'll start with creating a project, adding Verilog or VHDL sources, and selecting the correct MAX 10 device for the DE10‑Lite. Then you'll see how the compilation flow produces reports that tell you about resource usage and timing, and how viewers like the RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Chip Planner help you interpret synthesis and placement. Finally we'll walk through assigning input and output pins and programming the board with the USB‑Blaster. This matters because successfully moving from RTL to a running board requires more than code: it needs correct device selection, pin mapping, and validation using the viewers and reports. A concrete example we'll use throughout is building and compiling a 4‑bit counter for the DE10‑Lite, assigning its outputs to LEDs, and programming the board to verify operation. Anticipate common hiccups: wrong device family, missing pin assignments, or timing failures in the Timing Analyzer. By the end you'll understand the full Quartus Prime cycle and be ready to follow a step‑by‑step lab that compiles, views, and programs a design on hardware.

keyIdea.title: Overview
keyIdea.text: Quartus Prime integrates project creation, synthesis, place‑and‑route, visualization, and programming so you can go from HDL to running FPGA design on DE10‑Lite.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Using Quartus Prime
Using Quartus Prime for FPGA Development
From new project setup to programming the DE10‑Lite board and interpreting reports.
In this lesson

Create and configure projects, add HDL, compile and read reports, assign pins and use viewers to verify implementation. Finish by programming the FPGA.

Why it matters

Tool awareness and proper workflow prevent common mistakes such as wrong device selection, misplaced pins, and timing violations that block hardware testing.

Explore Key Topics
Project Wizard
Create .qpf/.qsf, add sources and choose EDA tools for simulation.
Compilation Flow
Analysis & Synthesis, Fitter, Assembler, and Timing Analyzer produce the reports you rely on.
Programming
Use the Programmer and USB‑Blaster to download a .sof file and run your design on the DE10‑Lite.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Project → Compile → Program
Example: 4‑bit counter
Count value mapped to LEDs, clock from 50 MHz oscillator, reset on a KEY pin, compile and program to verify binary counting on board.
Viewers
RTL Viewer for netlist sanity, Technology Map for actual LUT/FF mapping, Chip Planner for physical placement and routing inspection.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives frame the laboratory tasks and assessments you'll complete with Quartus Prime. First, you'll create and configure a new project, which includes generating the project files, choosing a directory, and adding HDL sources. A concrete example is making a project named BlinkLED and adding a Verilog file that defines a counter. Second, you'll select the target device and set pin assignments. For the DE10‑Lite that means choosing a MAX 10 device and mapping counter outputs to the documented LED pins. Third, you'll run a full compilation and interpret reports: Flow Summary, Fitter Summary, and Timing Analyzer tell you resource usage and whether your design meets timing. Finally, you'll use viewers — RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Chip Planner — to inspect how synthesis and place‑and‑route realized your code. Each objective matters because it connects a tool action to a hardware outcome. A common misconception is treating compilation as a single opaque step; instead, read each report to diagnose issues before programming the board. Practice these objectives in sequence to ensure your first board programming attempts succeed.

screens.title: Creating a New Quartus Project
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new Quartus Prime project is the first hands‑on step and it establishes the files and workspace the tool uses for synthesis and implementation. Use File → New Project Wizard to set a project directory and name; for example C colon backslash FPGA underscore Projects backslash BlinkLED. The wizard lets you add source files immediately or leave that for later; either is fine, but make sure any Verilog files are saved with a. v extension and VHDL with. vhd before you add them. The wizard also creates two key files: the. qpf which contains high‑level project settings and the. qsf which stores assignments like pin locations. A concrete example: create a project called BlinkLED, add a Verilog module that implements a counter, and finish the wizard to generate the project files. A common misconception is thinking the wizard writes pin assignments automatically — it does not. Pin mapping and device selection are separate steps. Why this matters: organized project files and correct source file types let Quartus find and synthesize your design cleanly. Before moving on, confirm the. qpf and. qsf exist and that your source appears under Project > Add/Remove Files in Project. That check prevents later missing‑source errors during compilation.

keyIdea.title: Project creation
keyIdea.text: The New Project Wizard establishes the .qpf and .qsf and records your initial sources; verify file creation and source registration before compiling.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Create Project
Steps
  1. Open File → New Project Wizard and choose the project directory and name.
  2. Add existing Verilog or VHDL source files, or create new ones with File → New.
  3. Select target device family and part number for your board.
  4. Choose EDA tool support for simulation, e.g., ModelSim‑Intel FPGA.
  5. Finish to generate .qpf and .qsf files in the project folder.
Example file names
C:\FPGA_Projects\BlinkLED\BlinkLED.qpf and BlinkLED.qsf and src\counter.v
Visual checks
Confirm project files
Verify .qpf and .qsf exist in the folder and your .v or .vhd sources are visible under Project → Add/Remove Files.
Common mistake
Adding a file with the wrong extension or a missing save causes "file not found" during synthesis.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Create the project early, ensure sources are saved with proper extensions, and confirm .qpf/.qsf presence to avoid compilation interruptions.

screens.title: Adding and Editing HDL Sources
screens.narratorSegment: Quartus Prime includes a built‑in text editor with syntax highlighting for Verilog and VHDL so you can create or modify RTL inside the tool. Start with File → New → Verilog HDL File or VHDL File, write your module, save it in the project folder, and add it via Project → Add/Remove Files in Project. A concrete example is a simple 4‑bit counter module saved as counter. v; keep your module and port names consistent with later pin assignments. When you edit code in Quartus, use meaningful signal names and modular structure so the RTL maps to readable netlist blocks in the RTL Viewer. A common misconception is that the editor changes are automatically included in the build; you must save the file and confirm it appears in the project sources. If you have external files, place them in the project directory or add them by absolute path but prefer project‑local sources for portability. As a practical tip, run a quick Analysis & Elaboration step after adding sources to check for syntax errors before full compilation. This approach reduces wasted time on the full flow and makes debugging faster.

keyIdea.title: Source authoring
keyIdea.text: Use Quartus' editor to write and save RTL, then add files to the project and run a syntax check before full compilation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › HDL Sources
Editor & workflow
Create a new Verilog or VHDL file, save it inside the project folder, and add it to the project. Always save before compilation and confirm the file is listed under Project → Add/Remove Files in Project.
Example Verilog
module counter(
  input clk,
  input rst,
  output reg [3:0] q
);

always @(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin
  if (rst)
    q <= 4'd0;
  else
    q <= q + 4'd1;
end

endmodule
Practical notes
  • Save files with correct extensions: .v for Verilog, .vhd for VHDL.
  • Add sources to the project; unsaved edits are not part of compilation.
  • Use Analysis & Synthesis as a quick syntax check before full build.
Common mistake
Forgetting to add the saved file to the project causes a silent omission: the design compiles without your new module or uses an old version.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Edit, save, and confirm source registration in the project to ensure your latest RTL is what Quartus compiles.

screens.title: Device Selection for DE10‑Lite
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct FPGA device in Quartus Prime is essential because the device selects available resources and the physical pinout the tool will reference. For the DE10‑Lite board you should pick a MAX 10 family and the specific part number 10M50DAF484C7G as shown in the chapter source. That selection determines the number of logic elements, memory bits, DSP blocks, and the exact naming of pins such as PIN_A8 for LED0. A common misconception is selecting a similar family or a generic device and assuming pin numbers remain valid; mismatched device selection leads to incorrect pin mappings and failed programming. Practical guidance: confirm the part number against the board documentation before configuring the project. If you later change the device, re‑run pin assignment checks and review the chip planner because placement constraints and available resources will differ. Example: selecting the DE10‑Lite's MAX 10 part ensures the Pin Planner shows the board's input and output bank and the USB‑Blaster will successfully target the device during programming. The key insight is this: device selection links your HDL to both logical resources and a physical pin map — get it right early to avoid downstream errors.

keyIdea.title: Device matters
keyIdea.text: Selecting the specific MAX 10 device for DE10‑Lite fixes resource availability and pin naming used throughout synthesis and pin planning.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Device Selection
Why part number matters
The exact part number determines the FPGA's logic and I/O resources. For DE10‑Lite use MAX 10 > 10M50DAF484C7G so pin names and resource limits match board documentation.
Comparison
Correct part
Matches board schematics and pin names, accurate resource counts.
Wrong/Generic part
Pin mismatches and incorrect fitter behavior; programming may fail.
Practical steps
  1. When creating the project, choose Device > Family: MAX 10 and select 10M50DAF484C7G.
  2. Confirm pin names in the Pin Planner match the DE10‑Lite user manual.
  3. If you change device later, revalidate all pin assignments and recompile.
Key Takeaway

Pick the exact MAX 10 part for DE10‑Lite at project setup so the toolchain uses the correct resource and pin definitions throughout the flow.

screens.title: Compilation Flow: From Analysis to Timing
screens.narratorSegment: Compilation in Quartus Prime is a multi‑stage process that transforms RTL into a bitstream you can program into the FPGA. The main stages are Analysis & Synthesis, Fitter, Assembler, and Timing Analyzer. Analysis & Synthesis converts your HDL into a generic netlist and reports initial resource usage. The Fitter places logic into the device and routes signals; its summary shows actual resource utilization and an estimated maximum clock frequency. The Assembler produces the programming file (. sof) that the Programmer downloads to the board. The Timing Analyzer computes detailed timing across all clock domains; it reports slack and whether your design meets timing constraints or has violations. A concrete example: after compiling a 4‑bit counter, the Flow Summary will show logic elements used and registers, Fitter Summary gives fmax, and Timing Analyzer confirms whether the 50 MHz clock meets timing. A common misconception is trusting only the Flow Summary; if Timing Analyzer shows negative slack, the design may not run at the target frequency even if synthesis and fitting completed. Always inspect the Timing Analyzer for each clock domain and use fmax and slack to guide optimizations or device selection. The takeaway: read reports at each stage to locate issues early and iterate efficiently.

keyIdea.title: Multi-stage compilation
keyIdea.text: Each compilation stage has a purpose and produces reports you must read: synthesis netlist, placement/resource usage, programming file, and timing verification.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Compilation Flow
Stages
Analysis & Synthesis: Converts HDL to a generic netlist and reports initial resource counts.
Fitter: Places logic into device resources, routes signals, and reports utilization and fmax.
Assembler: Generates the .sof file for programming the FPGA.
Timing Analyzer: Runs static timing analysis across clock domains and reports slack and violations.
Example outcome
Flow Summary: logic elements and registers used. Fitter Summary: resource distribution and estimated fmax. Timing Analyzer: per‑domain timing and slack values.
Reading reports
  • Look for resource counts exceeding device capacity or unusually high usage percentages.
  • Check fmax for the clock domains and compare with your system requirements.
  • Address negative slack in Timing Analyzer before programming the board.
Key Takeaway

Treat compilation as an analyzable pipeline: use each report to find and fix issues rather than guessing why a design fails on hardware.

screens.title: Interpreting Compilation Reports
screens.narratorSegment: Compilation reports are your diagnostic instruments after a build completes. The Flow Summary gives an overview: total logic elements, registers, memory bits, and DSP usage. That report quickly tells you if the design exceeds device capacity. Fitter Summary dives deeper into how logic maps to physical resources and provides an estimated maximum clock frequency, fmax. Timing Analyzer performs static timing analysis and reports timing paths, slack, and whether constraints are met. A concrete example: if your 4‑bit counter is lightly using logic elements but Timing Analyzer reports negative slack at a high clock rate, it means your path delays or constraints prevent meeting that frequency even though resources are available. A common misconception is to focus only on absolute resource counts; resource usage can be acceptable while timing still fails. Use the reports together: Flow Summary for capacity, Fitter Summary for mapping and fmax, and Timing Analyzer for detailed path timing. When you see high utilization percentages or timing violations, your options include RTL optimization, using hard blocks like memory/DSP if applicable, or selecting a larger device. The core idea is to read the reports to direct targeted fixes instead of trial‑and‑error recompiles.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Compilation Reports
Flow Summary
Shows totals: logic elements, registers, memory bits, DSP blocks. Use this first to check capacity.
Fitter Summary
Displays resource distribution after placement and routing and provides an fmax estimate for the design.
Timing Analyzer
Performs static timing checks and reports slack and failing paths for each clock domain.
Actionable checks
  • If Flow Summary shows >100% utilization, consider design optimization or larger device.
  • If Fitter shows low slack or low fmax, explore critical path restructuring or reduce logic depth on the clocked path.
  • If Timing Analyzer reports negative slack, identify failing nets and constraints, then iterate RTL or constraints.
Common-mistake

Treating reports in isolation. Read all three reports together to understand whether issues are resource or timing related, and choose the right remediation path.

screens.title: Pin Assignments and the Pin Planner
screens.narratorSegment: Assigning ports to physical pins is required before programming hardware. Quartus Prime provides the Pin Planner under Assignments → Pin Planner where you find your port names and enter the matching pin locations such as PIN_A8 for LED0. The DE10‑Lite user manual documents which pins connect to board peripherals: LEDs, switches, and the 50 MHz clock. You can double‑click a Location cell to type a pin name or use a Tcl script to set_location_assignment lines for automation. An example Tcl snippet from the chapter maps LED and KEY pins and the clock; using a script is helpful when multiple pins or boards are involved, and it ensures repeatable assignments across projects. A common misconception is that default or inferred pins are correct; they rarely match a specific board. After assigning pins, save the. qsf file; it records your assignments and can be edited directly if needed. Before programming, confirm in the Chip Planner that the assigned pins align with actual input and output banks. The key practical step is to validate your pin plan against the board schematics so that the compiled bitstream drives the intended physical connectors.

keyIdea.title: Pin planning
keyIdea.text: Use the Pin Planner or .qsf/Tcl to assign HDL ports to board‑documented pins and save assignments before compiling and programming.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Pin Planner
Pin Planner steps
  1. Open Assignments → Pin Planner and locate your module port names.
  2. Double‑click the Location column and enter the PIN name from the board schematic, e.g., PIN_A8 for LED0.
  3. Save assignments to update the project's .qsf file.
  4. Optionally script assignments with Tcl for repeatability.
Example Tcl
set_location_assignment PIN_A8 -to LED[0]
set_location_assignment PIN_A9 -to LED[1]
set_location_assignment PIN_A10 -to LED[2]
set_location_assignment PIN_A11 -to LED[3]
set_location_assignment PIN_A12 -to LED[4]
set_location_assignment PIN_A13 -to LED[5]
set_location_assignment PIN_A14 -to LED[6]
set_location_assignment PIN_A15 -to LED[7]
set_location_assignment PIN_B8 -to KEY[0]
set_location_assignment PIN_B9 -to KEY[1]
set_location_assignment PIN_P11 -to CLK
Validation
After assigning pins, open Chip Planner to verify the pins are placed in the expected I/O banks and check for conflicts or bank voltage mismatches.
Key Takeaway

Pin assignments are a hardware mapping. Always confirm assignments against the board's documentation and save them in the .qsf or via a Tcl script for reproducibility.

screens.title: Design Visualization: RTL Viewer
screens.narratorSegment: The RTL Viewer displays the generic netlist produced during synthesis, showing how your HDL translates into gates, multiplexers, and flip‑flops before technology mapping. Use it to verify that synthesis captured the architectural intent of your RTL. For example, if you write a register with a synchronous reset, the RTL Viewer should show a flip‑flop with the reset path; if it shows unexpected combinational logic, you've likely written unintended constructs in your code. A common misconception is to use the RTL Viewer to inspect mapped LUTs — it intentionally shows the generic, technology‑independent netlist. For mapping details and actual LUT/FF usage, use the Technology Map Viewer after fitting. Practically, open Tools → Netlist Viewers → RTL Viewer once Analysis & Synthesis completes and inspect the schematic that corresponds to your top module. This step is invaluable the first time you synthesize a new module because it catches synthesis misunderstandings early without waiting for the full fit and place‑and‑route. Ask yourself: does this netlist reflect the architectural structure I intended? Design Visualization: RTL Viewer means rtl viewer helps confirm synthesis interpreted your hdl as intended by showing a generic netlist before technology mapping.. In practical terms, verify that synthesis correctly interpreted your hdl. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › RTL Viewer
What it shows
A technology‑independent netlist showing registers, combinational logic, and connectivity. Use it to verify synthesis produced the structure you intended from your HDL.
When to use
  • After Analysis & Synthesis to confirm module structure.
  • To check reset and clocking behavior represented by flip‑flops.
  • To spot unintended logic resulting from coding mistakes.
Checklist
  • Does the RTL netlist reflect your module hierarchy?
  • Are registers and reset paths present as expected?
  • Do combinational blocks match intended logic expressions?
Common-mistake

Expecting to see technology-mapped LUTs in the RTL Viewer. Use Technology Map Viewer for post‑mapping details.

screens.title: Technology Map Viewer & Chip Planner
screens.narratorSegment: After fitting, the Technology Map Viewer shows how the synthesis netlist was mapped to actual device primitives: LUTs, flip‑flops, carry chains, and other blocks. Use it to identify inefficient mapping or to find where logic clustered in the device. The Chip Planner complements this by presenting the physical layout on the FPGA die so you can inspect which CLBs and routing resources your design uses and where input and output pins are placed. For example, if a critical register cluster ends up far from the clock buffer, you may see timing pressure that the Timing Analyzer will report. A common misconception is that placement is invisible; Chip Planner makes physical placement explicit and helps debug placement‑related routing congestion. Practically, open Tools → Netlist Viewers → Technology Map Viewer (Post‑Mapping) and then Tools → Chip Planner to compare logical mapping to physical placement. These viewers are most useful when you are tracking down timing violations or trying to optimize resource locality. The key insight is that mapping and placement directly affect timing, so visualization helps you prioritize RTL changes or floorplanning decisions.

Technology Map Viewer
Shows LUTs, FFs, carry chains and how the generic netlist maps to device primitives after technology mapping. Use it to spot inefficient logic implementations.
Chip Planner
Displays physical placement on the die and the routing between used CLBs and I/O. Useful for diagnosing placement‑related timing issues and verifying pin placements.
When to inspect
  • After fitting when timing issues remain unresolved.

screens.title: Programming the DE10‑Lite
screens.narratorSegment: Programming the FPGA is the final step to run your compiled design on hardware. Connect the DE10‑Lite to your computer via USB and open Tools → Programmer in Quartus Prime. Click Hardware Setup and select USB‑Blaster, then Auto Detect to enumerate the device. In the Programmer window, right‑click the device entry and Change File to choose the. sof file produced by the Assembler in the output_files directory. Check the Program/Configure box and click Start to download the bitstream to the FPGA; the design will begin running immediately. Note that many MAX 10 devices use SRAM for the logic fabric, so configuration is lost on power‑off unless you program the on‑chip flash using a. pof file to store a persistent configuration. A common mistake is using the wrong file type:. sof for immediate configuration of volatile logic,. pof for programming flash. After programming, verify behavior using the board LEDs and switches — for example, confirm the 4‑bit counter increments on the LED bank and reset responds to the KEY pin. If programming fails, check the Hardware Setup, confirm the correct device is selected, and revalidate pin assignments in the. qsf. Successful programming completes the full Quartus Prime to‑hardware cycle.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Program FPGA
Programmer steps
  1. Connect DE10‑Lite via USB and open Tools → Programmer.
  2. Click Hardware Setup, select USB‑Blaster, then Auto Detect.
  3. Right‑click device → Change File and select the .sof from output_files.

Use .sof for immediate volatile configuration. Use .pof to program on‑chip flash when a persistent configuration is required.

After programming, verify the design runs: for the counter example, LEDs should increment in binary and KEY reset should clear the counter.

Programming completes the cycle. Confirm USB‑Blaster connectivity and choose .sof for testing, .pof for permanent flash programming when needed.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll develop a practical workflow for using Intel Quartus Prime to build and deploy FPGA designs. We'll start with creating a project, adding Verilog or VHDL sources, and selecting the correct MAX 10 device for the DE10‑Lite. Then you'll see how the compilation flow produces reports that tell you about resource usage and timing, and how viewers like the RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Chip Planner help you interpret synthesis and placement. Finally we'll walk through assigning input and output pins and programming the board with the USB‑Blaster. This matters because successfully moving from RTL to a running board requires more than code: it needs correct device selection, pin mapping, and validation using the viewers and reports. A concrete example we'll use throughout is building and compiling a 4‑bit counter for the DE10‑Lite, assigning its outputs to LEDs, and programming the board to verify operation. Anticipate common hiccups: wrong device family, missing pin assignments, or timing failures in the Timing Analyzer. By the end you'll understand the full Quartus Prime cycle and be ready to follow a step‑by‑step lab that compiles, views, and programs a design on hardware.

These learning objectives frame the laboratory tasks and assessments you'll complete with Quartus Prime. First, you'll create and configure a new project, which includes generating the project files, choosing a directory, and adding HDL sources. A concrete example is making a project named BlinkLED and adding a Verilog file that defines a counter. Second, you'll select the target device and set pin assignments. For the DE10‑Lite that means choosing a MAX 10 device and mapping counter outputs to the documented LED pins. Third, you'll run a full compilation and interpret reports: Flow Summary, Fitter Summary, and Timing Analyzer tell you resource usage and whether your design meets timing. Finally, you'll use viewers — RTL Viewer, Technology Map Viewer, and Chip Planner — to inspect how synthesis and place‑and‑route realized your code. Each objective matters because it connects a tool action to a hardware outcome. A common misconception is treating compilation as a single opaque step; instead, read each report to diagnose issues before programming the board. Practice these objectives in sequence to ensure your first board programming attempts succeed.

This second objectives screen frames evidence you should produce in the lab. For project setup, demonstrate a project directory with a. qpf and. qsf file and at least one added HDL source saved with the correct extension. For device selection and pin mapping, show the chosen MAX 10 device entry for DE10‑Lite and a Pin Planner listing that maps LED and KEY ports to documented pin names. For compilation analysis, export or screenshot the Flow Summary with resource counts and the Timing Analyzer showing fmax or timing violations. For visualization, open the RTL Viewer and Technology Map Viewer, capture a view that connects your HDL construct to mapped LUTs or flip‑flops, and show Chip Planner placement for a small design. These deliverables turn abstract skills into verifiable artifacts. A common mistake is skipping the viewers when compilation succeeds; always inspect netlists and placement to ensure the synthesized hardware matches your intent.

Creating a new Quartus Prime project is the first hands‑on step and it establishes the files and workspace the tool uses for synthesis and implementation. Use File → New Project Wizard to set a project directory and name; for example C colon backslash FPGA underscore Projects backslash BlinkLED. The wizard lets you add source files immediately or leave that for later; either is fine, but make sure any Verilog files are saved with a. v extension and VHDL with. vhd before you add them. The wizard also creates two key files: the. qpf which contains high‑level project settings and the. qsf which stores assignments like pin locations. A concrete example: create a project called BlinkLED, add a Verilog module that implements a counter, and finish the wizard to generate the project files. A common misconception is thinking the wizard writes pin assignments automatically — it does not. Pin mapping and device selection are separate steps. Why this matters: organized project files and correct source file types let Quartus find and synthesize your design cleanly. Before moving on, confirm the. qpf and. qsf exist and that your source appears under Project > Add/Remove Files in Project. That check prevents later missing‑source errors during compilation.

Quartus Prime includes a built‑in text editor with syntax highlighting for Verilog and VHDL so you can create or modify RTL inside the tool. Start with File → New → Verilog HDL File or VHDL File, write your module, save it in the project folder, and add it via Project → Add/Remove Files in Project. A concrete example is a simple 4‑bit counter module saved as counter. v; keep your module and port names consistent with later pin assignments. When you edit code in Quartus, use meaningful signal names and modular structure so the RTL maps to readable netlist blocks in the RTL Viewer. A common misconception is that the editor changes are automatically included in the build; you must save the file and confirm it appears in the project sources. If you have external files, place them in the project directory or add them by absolute path but prefer project‑local sources for portability. As a practical tip, run a quick Analysis & Elaboration step after adding sources to check for syntax errors before full compilation. This approach reduces wasted time on the full flow and makes debugging faster.

Choosing the correct FPGA device in Quartus Prime is essential because the device selects available resources and the physical pinout the tool will reference. For the DE10‑Lite board you should pick a MAX 10 family and the specific part number 10M50DAF484C7G as shown in the chapter source. That selection determines the number of logic elements, memory bits, DSP blocks, and the exact naming of pins such as PIN_A8 for LED0. A common misconception is selecting a similar family or a generic device and assuming pin numbers remain valid; mismatched device selection leads to incorrect pin mappings and failed programming. Practical guidance: confirm the part number against the board documentation before configuring the project. If you later change the device, re‑run pin assignment checks and review the chip planner because placement constraints and available resources will differ. Example: selecting the DE10‑Lite's MAX 10 part ensures the Pin Planner shows the board's input and output bank and the USB‑Blaster will successfully target the device during programming. The key insight is this: device selection links your HDL to both logical resources and a physical pin map — get it right early to avoid downstream errors.

Compilation in Quartus Prime is a multi‑stage process that transforms RTL into a bitstream you can program into the FPGA. The main stages are Analysis & Synthesis, Fitter, Assembler, and Timing Analyzer. Analysis & Synthesis converts your HDL into a generic netlist and reports initial resource usage. The Fitter places logic into the device and routes signals; its summary shows actual resource utilization and an estimated maximum clock frequency. The Assembler produces the programming file (. sof) that the Programmer downloads to the board. The Timing Analyzer computes detailed timing across all clock domains; it reports slack and whether your design meets timing constraints or has violations. A concrete example: after compiling a 4‑bit counter, the Flow Summary will show logic elements used and registers, Fitter Summary gives fmax, and Timing Analyzer confirms whether the 50 MHz clock meets timing. A common misconception is trusting only the Flow Summary; if Timing Analyzer shows negative slack, the design may not run at the target frequency even if synthesis and fitting completed. Always inspect the Timing Analyzer for each clock domain and use fmax and slack to guide optimizations or device selection. The takeaway: read reports at each stage to locate issues early and iterate efficiently.

Compilation reports are your diagnostic instruments after a build completes. The Flow Summary gives an overview: total logic elements, registers, memory bits, and DSP usage. That report quickly tells you if the design exceeds device capacity. Fitter Summary dives deeper into how logic maps to physical resources and provides an estimated maximum clock frequency, fmax. Timing Analyzer performs static timing analysis and reports timing paths, slack, and whether constraints are met. A concrete example: if your 4‑bit counter is lightly using logic elements but Timing Analyzer reports negative slack at a high clock rate, it means your path delays or constraints prevent meeting that frequency even though resources are available. A common misconception is to focus only on absolute resource counts; resource usage can be acceptable while timing still fails. Use the reports together: Flow Summary for capacity, Fitter Summary for mapping and fmax, and Timing Analyzer for detailed path timing. When you see high utilization percentages or timing violations, your options include RTL optimization, using hard blocks like memory/DSP if applicable, or selecting a larger device. The core idea is to read the reports to direct targeted fixes instead of trial‑and‑error recompiles.

Assigning ports to physical pins is required before programming hardware. Quartus Prime provides the Pin Planner under Assignments → Pin Planner where you find your port names and enter the matching pin locations such as PIN_A8 for LED0. The DE10‑Lite user manual documents which pins connect to board peripherals: LEDs, switches, and the 50 MHz clock. You can double‑click a Location cell to type a pin name or use a Tcl script to set_location_assignment lines for automation. An example Tcl snippet from the chapter maps LED and KEY pins and the clock; using a script is helpful when multiple pins or boards are involved, and it ensures repeatable assignments across projects. A common misconception is that default or inferred pins are correct; they rarely match a specific board. After assigning pins, save the. qsf file; it records your assignments and can be edited directly if needed. Before programming, confirm in the Chip Planner that the assigned pins align with actual input and output banks. The key practical step is to validate your pin plan against the board schematics so that the compiled bitstream drives the intended physical connectors.
